article_title: Content-Focused Coaching — Whole Class
citation: Content-Focused Coaching. (2023). Content-Focused Coaching. Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Question-the-Author literacy pattern: students question texts and challenge each other's interpretations
description: The literacy strategies used in CFC are drawn from Question the Author: teachers pose questions to students to promote understanding, interpretation, and active response. Students are encouraged to challenge each other's interpretations and to challenge the authors, identifying places in texts where they want to know more. This pattern positions students as active interrogators of text meaning rather than passive recipients.
requirements: Teachers learn to pose questions to students to promote understanding, interpretation, and active response
target_learners: Fourth and fifth grade students
English learners
target_learning_goals: Text understanding, interpretation, and active response
examples: Students identify places in texts in which they want to know more and challenge each other's interpretations during CFC-supported literacy lessons.

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Quartile-benchmarked category reporting format compares a school's responses to bottom- and top-quartile schools with defined category descriptions
description: Each measure is reported as a horizontal bar figure showing the percentage of respondents endorsing each survey item, with a diamond marking the systemwide average, followed by a frequency distribution placing the school's responses among four defined categories alongside bottom-quartile and top-quartile schools. Schools are divided 'into four equally sized categories (quartiles) based on their responses to each set of questions,' and each category (e.g., minimal, limited, moderate, extensive) is defined in detail in an accompanying table. Bars exceeding 65 percent extend to the top of the axis without a value label.
requirements: A sufficient response rate for the school and item-level response counts to compute percentages
constraints: The schools in each quartile varied for every set of questions, so a school can be top quartile on one measure and bottom quartile on another; bars above 65 percent are not given value labels
target_learners: school principals, teachers, and Local School Councils conducting self-assessment
target_learning_goals: interpreting school climate and instructional program measures
examples: For Teacher Influence, the report explains that 23 percent of teachers in bottom-quartile schools considered their influence minimal, compared with 4 percent in top-quartile schools and 9 percent in the sample school
key_sources: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-sample-high-school-details-2005

citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). title: Make visible improvements early in the turnaround process (quick wins)
description: Early in a turnaround, the school should pursue a goal that is important, achievable quickly, and visibly improved, because quick wins "can rally staff around the effort and overcome resistance and inertia." The strategy should be implementable quickly, for example when the school already has the authority and resources to act.
requirements: Start with a goal that is important, can be achieved quickly, and will provide visible improvement, with a strategy the school can implement quickly
constraints: Signaling change without following through with quick wins could make school staff skeptical
target_learners: students and staff in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: building staff commitment and momentum for schoolwide improvement
examples: Common quick-win goals named in the guide include changing the school's use of time, improving access to resources and physical facilities, and improving discipline

article_title: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Six design characteristics of rigorous and meaningful micro-credentials
description: The eBook enumerates the characteristics that distinguish the most rigorous and meaningful micro-credentials from lower-quality offerings. They are "Competency-based", articulating a discrete skill and the evidence required; research-backed; personalized, letting learners choose credentials aligned to their goals and pace; on-demand; shareable on resumes and profiles; and recognizing, honoring skills "regardless of when, how, and where they were attained", including prior learning. The pattern cautions that quality varies across the field, so these characteristics serve as design and selection criteria.
requirements: Each micro-credential must articulate a discrete skill, the specific evidence to submit, and be grounded in research illustrating how the competency supports positive professional impact
constraints: The quality of micro-credentials varies; these characteristics describe the most rigorous and meaningful subset
target_learners: Lifelong learners
Educators
Workforce learners
target_learning_goals: Recognition of specific, in-demand skills aligned to career goals
examples: Digital Promise's own credentials embody the pattern, being individually assessed by a subject matter expert and awarded as Open Badges with secure metadata

description: El eBook enumera las características que hacen que una micro-credencial sea rigurosa y significativa: "Las micro-credenciales se basan en competencias, son personalizables, se pueden compartir, están respaldadas por investigación, son evaluadas individualmente por un experto en la materia y se otorgan en función de la demostración satisfactoria de una destreza". article_title: Preschool Quality and Child Development: How Are Learning Gains Related to Program Ratings?
citation: Sussman, J., Melnick, H., Newton, E., Kriener-Althen, K., Draney, K., Mangione, P., & Gochyyev, P. (2022). Preschool quality and child development: How are learning gains related to program ratings? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/422.974
title: Quality Counts California (QCC) quality rating and improvement system
description: Quality Counts California is a quality rating and improvement system, a collaboration between First 5 California, the California Department of Education, and the California Department of Social Services. Early learning and care sites are rated on seven elements and assigned a final quality rating in a tiering system ranging from Tier 1 (lowest) to Tier 5 (highest). The seven elements are child observation; developmental and health screenings; lead teacher qualifications; teacher–child interactions; teacher–child ratios and group size; program environment rating scales; and director qualifications, with ratings assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations. Participation is voluntary; 28% of licensed early learning centers participated during the 2020–21 funding year.
requirements: Ratings are assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations
constraints: Participation in QCC is voluntary
target_learners: preschool children ages 4.5 to 5.5 in publicly funded early learning programs
target_learning_goals: early learning and development across social-emotional, language and literacy, and mathematics domains
examples: The study analyzed QCC ratings alongside DRDP scores for approximately 70,000 children in 1,700 rated programs

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: Quantway College with Corequisite and Statway College with Corequisite one-term course sets
description: Two one-term course sets developed by the Carnegie Math Pathways for corequisite remediation, each pairing a college-level course with a developmental-level corequisite. As the report describes them, "Each is designed as a one-term stand-alone course set: a college-level course with some embedded learning supports and a corresponding corequisite course that provides learners with additional support." Both courses in each pair use the pedagogy and learning supports of the original two-term pathway courses, and developmental-level lessons were designed to be independent so faculty can skip lessons. Institutions could use separate or single enrollment, and contact hours for the pair ranged from four to six across the six implementing institutions.
requirements: Faculty time before each course pair starts to review lessons, select content, and structure course timelines to fit the local implementation configuration
constraints: Learning must take place in a shorter time frame than the two-term pathways, and faculty reported too little time for student learning as the chief challenge
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics at two-year and four-year institutions
target_learning_goals: College-level quantitative reasoning or statistics credit earned in a single term
examples: Six institutions delivered the offerings via 15 faculty across 21 sections reaching 410 students in spring 2018 and fall 2018

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Design education investments with sufficient quality, intensity, duration, and dosage to yield strong benefit-cost ratios
description: The report's economic evaluations indicate that intervention design features drive returns: "the quality, intensity, and duration of the interventions are important, as higher benefit-to-cost ratios are usually associated with more resource-intense programs and those with stronger dosage effects and/or with longer exposure." This principle directs policymakers and program designers to resource interventions adequately rather than scaling back inputs, since under-resourced versions may fail to reproduce the returns documented in evaluations.
requirements: Programs must be funded and implemented at the quality, intensity, and duration levels associated with higher benefit-to-cost ratios in the evaluation literature
constraints: Higher benefit-to-cost ratios are associated with more resource-intense programs, implying greater upfront cost
target_learners: All students, with particular benefit for the most disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: Maximizing net economic and educational returns on educational investment
examples: The report's synthesis of economic evaluations found stronger dosage effects and longer exposure linked to higher returns.

citation: Ahangama. (2026). Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00582-0
title: Quality gatekeeping: securing critical stage-gate assessments rather than every task
description: This pattern concentrates heightened assessment security at critical program-level checkpoints such as capstone projects, demonstrations, or milestone evaluations, rather than attempting to secure every assessment against GenAI. The article reports that "securing every assessment task against GenAI is both unrealistic and undesirable; instead, programs should identify critical stage-gates" where security is necessary, enabling earlier detection of learning gaps and consistent program standards.
requirements: Program-level identification of key assessment moments
Coordination across the program rather than unit-level decisions
constraints: Securing every task is described as unrealistic and undesirable
target_learners: ICT tertiary students
target_learning_goals: Verifying essential knowledge and competencies before progression or graduation
examples: One document described the approach as identifying the key assessment moments at a program level and securing those

article_title: LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments
citation: Xiomara Gonzalez, Gabriella Coloyan Fleming, Andrew Katz, Maya Denton, Jessica Deters. (2026). LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments. https://www.google.com/search?q=LLM-assisted+sentiment+analysis+for+integrated+computational+and+qualitative+mixed+methods+education+research
title: Quasi-mixed methods: an LLM-human workflow applying quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset
description: The article proposes a "quasi-mixed" method in which "our “quasi-mixed” method applies quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset", extending NLP-human mixed-methods workflows to an LLM-human workflow. It is operationalized as a six-stage pipeline: data familiarization, manual quote extraction, human and LLM-assisted sentiment labeling, human revision of LLM labels, parallel qualitative and quantitative analyses, and interpretation of qualitative findings considering quantitative results. The LLM is treated as an additional individual rater whose discrepancies inform deeper analysis.
requirements: Manually extracted quotes for downstream tasks, since the model's own quote extraction was unreliable
Human review of LLM sentiment labels to resolve discrepancies and ensure analytic coherence
Iterative prompt tuning and Python scripts to automate model inference and track outputs
constraints: Prompt designs are dataset- and context-specific, limiting generalizability across research settings
Upfront technical setup and administrative overhead may outweigh payoff for smaller datasets or single-use analyses
Only open source models were ethically usable because participants did not consent to data sharing with third-party commercial entities
target_learners: Undergraduate engineering students in study abroad programs
Education researchers analyzing qualitative reflection data
target_learning_goals: Cross-cultural communication skills
Critical self-assessment and meaning-making through written reflection
examples: The pipeline was applied to 535 quotations from 51 students across three reflection time points, partitioned by seven student identities and lived experiences, using MetaAI's Llama3 model (8 billion parameters) run locally via the Ollama framework with temperature set to 0

article_title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Qualitative orientation state vector and transition matrix for stair-blocks
description: Blocks in the model carry a qualitative orientation descriptor: 'The vectorO= (Axis,f,ι)governs the spatial projection and parity of the block via three qualitative operations' — Axis (horizontal/vertical), Reflection (mirroring) and Inversion (flipping). Table 1 enumerates the resulting orientation labels (HN, HM, HNI, HMI, VN, VM, VNI, VMI, RB) with their functional affordances, and Table 2 defines how orientations change under Reflect, Invert and Transpose operations, pruning illegal states such as inverted vertical pillars. The solver uses this matrix to explore valid placements during backtracking.

Illegal orientations (e.g., VNI and VMI) must be pruned per game rules
constraints: For rectangular blocks only to-and-fro Horizontal-Vertical state transitions exist
target_learners: game-playing AI agents
children solving block-puzzle challenges
target_learning_goals: reasoning about block orientations and affordances
planning legal placements
examples: Figure 2 schematizes the eight qualitative orientation states for a stair-block, with VNI and VMI marked illegal

article_title: Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation
citation: Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer, Moriah Ariely, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Asaf Salman, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07647v2
title: Quality-conditioned fairness: automated scoring must maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality
description: Quality-conditioned fairness is the standard the article proposes for evaluating automated scoring: "the requirement that automated scoring systems maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality". The article grounds it empirically: scoring errors concentrate on mid-range responses "typically produced by students whose knowledge is still developing", who may benefit most from formative feedback, making mid-range inaccuracy a fairness concern rather than mere noise.
requirements: states of knowledge must be detected accurately and equitably so that learners at different current states receive appropriate learning support rather than inappropriate help
constraints: the article shows current few-shot LLM scoring violates this standard in the mid-range; generalizability beyond the two biology items remains to be established
target_learners: high-school biology students (grades 10-12)
students with developing (partial) understanding
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable scoring of open-ended scientific explanations
formative feedback targeting partially correct understanding
examples: the article turns mid-range degradation from an unknown bias into a known bias, a step it describes as necessary toward improving fairness in educational AI

citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Quality-matched feedback design: LLM adaptive feedback versus expert generic guidance materials
description: The study released a web-based feedback provider system, six scenario-based planning tasks, five expert-written generic guidance versions, a Chain-of-Thought prompt for GPT-4-generated adaptive feedback, and a five-dimension feedback quality rubric (specificity, suggestions, explanation, remarks, formulation). Both conditions were "equivalent in instructional purpose, structure, tone, length, and complexity", differing only in response-contingent adaptation. All materials are publicly available on the OSF.

article_title: When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms
citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046
title: Qualitative meta-synthesis as a method for reconciling divergent meta-analyses of PBL effectiveness
description: The article's organizing approach is a qualitative meta-synthesis: rather than computing a new pooled estimate, it compares and contrasts the assumptions and findings of existing meta-analyses of PBL. The method treats divergent meta-analytic conclusions as data, explaining apparent contradictions (e.g., retention outcomes) by the type of outcome measured. As the article states, "This study used a qualitative meta-synthesis approach to compare and contrast the assumptions and findings of the meta-analytical research on the effectiveness of PBL."
requirements: Requires a body of existing meta-analyses on the topic whose assumptions and findings can be compared and contrasted
constraints: Conclusions are qualitative syntheses of prior meta-analyses rather than new pooled effect estimates
target_learners: students in PBL and conventional classrooms across disciplines
target_learning_goals: long-term retention, skill development, short-term retention on standardized exams
examples: The synthesis reconciled meta-analytic disagreement by showing PBL advantages on long-term retention, skill development, and satisfaction, and traditional-instruction advantages on short-term board-exam retention.

article_title: Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study
citation: Aline Godfroid, Jieun Ahn, Ina Choi, Laura Ballard, Yaqiong Cui, Suzanne Johnston, Shinhye Lee, Abdhi Sarkar and Hyung-Jo Yoon (2017). Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, Volume 21, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728917000219
title: Quantity and quality of lexical processing jointly drive incremental vocabulary development
description: The article advances an account in which two aspects of lexical processing during reading support incidental vocabulary growth: quantity, indexed by number of exposures, and quality, indexed by total reading time. The authors conclude that "both quantity and quality of lexical processing aid incremental vocabulary development" and that the two "may reveal themselves differently in readers’ eye movement records", so different eye-movement measures capture different aspects of processing.
requirements: Eye-movement records from natural reading of connected text
Vocabulary learning measured for both word form and word meaning
constraints: The account is drawn from a single eye-tracking study in which participants read one authentic novel in two sessions.
target_learners: native and non-native English speakers reading authentic texts
target_learning_goals: incidental vocabulary learning of word form and meaning
examples: Growth curve modeling of eye-tracking data during novel reading linked exposure count to form and meaning learning and total reading time to meaning learning

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Quality-script development: evaluative judgement grows through staged expertise from analytical to pattern-based judgement
description: The paper hypothesises, drawing on the staged theory of expertise of decision-making (Schmidt and Rikers 2007), that students develop "quality scripts" analogous to illness scripts in medical training. Through repeated exposure to work, consideration of standards, and justification of decisions, knowledge about quality becomes linked and chunked into patterns, so judgement becomes less analytical and more intuitive, with analytical reasoning retained as a safety mechanism for non-fitting problems.
requirements: Repeated practice making evaluative judgements in different situations, with justification of decisions in relation to knowledge and standards
constraints: The account is a hypothesis the authors propose by analogy to medical decision-making expertise, not an empirically tested result
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: developing domain-specific judgement of quality
examples: Medical trainees chunk biomedical knowledge with clinical signs into illness scripts, making decisions less analytical as experience grows
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Integrating ChatGPT in Grade 12 Quantum Theory Education: An Exploratory Study at Emirate School (UAE)
citation: Saif Alneyadi and Yousef Wardat. (2024). Integrating ChatGPT in Grade 12 Quantum Theory Education: An Exploratory Study at Emirate School (UAE). International Journal of Information and Education Technology, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://doi.org/10.18178/ijiet.2024.14.3.2061
title: Quantum Theory Test: a 30-item achievement test organized into Knowing, Applying, and Reasoning sections built on Bloom's taxonomy
description: The study's achievement instrument is "a single form of the test" of 30 questions organized into three sections of ten questions each (Knowing, Applying, Reasoning), crafted using Bloom's taxonomy levels from remembering to creating. Validity was checked by a panel of UAE expert arbitrators, and a pilot found discrimination coefficients of 0.35–0.72 and difficulty coefficients of 0.50–0.77. It measured pre- and post-test achievement in both study groups.
requirements: Validated by expert arbitrators in education, measurement, and evaluation, with item revision based on their feedback and a pilot study to establish item difficulty and discrimination

article_title: Quasi-communities: rethinking learning in formal adult and vocational education
citation: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9
title: Quasi-community framework for theorizing learning in formal adult and vocational education
description: A quasi-community is an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context, retaining dimensions of communities of practice while abandoning others. The article defines it as "an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context that lacks the essentially spatiotemporal nature of relations within true communities." Unlike true communities, it has "no noticeable core and periphery": mastery is relative, dynamically distributed, and any member can act as old-timer or newcomer depending on the task at hand. The framework was developed and illustrated through a case study of mariners in formal certification training.
requirements: A common object/motive shared by members must be realized early for the community to form
constraints: The concept addresses formal adult and vocational settings where classes are administratively formed and disbanded after short periods, so collective memory is temporally limited

target_learning_goals: Domain competency development for certification and workplace practice

citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2

citation: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Use scale points as a quantitative, not rigidly qualitative, measure of retention in a school subject

article_title: The Effect of Question-Generation Strategy on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Development
citation: Khansir, A. A., & Dashti, J. G. (2014). The Effect of Question-Generation Strategy on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Development. English Language Teaching, 7(4), 38-44. http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n4p38
title: Question-generation strategy rests on three essential elements: active processing, metacognitive processing, and schema processing
description: The article organizes the question-generation strategy around three essential elements. Active processing holds that "students become active readers and independent thinkers via generating questions in order to understand the text" (Wong, 1985). Metacognitive processing involves planning, monitoring, and evaluating one's comprehension, so learners become aware of comprehension gaps. Schema processing holds that readers with rich prior knowledge comprehend text better than those with weak background.
requirements: Students must generate questions based on reading content, using formats such as multiple-choice, matching, short answer, true-false, and fill-in-the-blank.
constraints: The article notes that inadequate word knowledge of learners constrained the rhetorical text types that could be used.
target_learners: Iranian third-grade high school EFL students
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of English passages

Willingness to adjust revision format to the number of students with problems

Timely identification and remediation of mispronunciations
examples: In the study, the Quiz step used flashcards of the target phonemes administered individually, in group, or classically, and Revision treated one or two students individually, some in group, and most classically.

title: Question the structures of prejudice rather than teaching tolerance as a rule
description: Because teaching tolerance as a subject can itself engender intolerance, the authors adopted processes that question the structures of intolerance, so that tolerance can evolve as students notice discrepancies in the foundations of their prejudice. The classroom, with its communicative opportunities in the English Language class, serves as the setting for this critical appraisal rather than direct tolerance instruction.

Flexibility in classroom activities and learning contents
constraints: Several factors are at play in the classroom and beyond that the teacher may not control

critical thinking

title: Qualitative meta-synthesis as a methodology for synthesizing reflection research
description: The article describes qualitative meta-synthesis as an approach that synthesizes qualitative studies to achieve "interpretative explanations of the phenomenon" rather than aggregating findings. It involves six phases: conception of synthesis, identifying target studies, reading and evaluating studies, drawing links between studies, synthesizing studies, and presenting the synthesis. The approach acknowledges that experiences are constructed and understood from multiple perspectives.
requirements: Careful selection of topically similar studies (about 10 recommended)
Comparison of methodologies across selected studies
Dialectic analysis to determine links between constructs
constraints: Relying on a sample size that is too large will hamper deep analyses
Researchers must account for differences and not aggregate studies unnecessarily
target_learners: Researchers studying reflection in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding reflection across disciplines and contexts
examples: The authors applied the six-phase procedure informed by Aspfors and Fransson (2015) to synthesize ten qualitative studies of student reflection

description: The article argues that teachers can use well-designed curriculum materials, along with guidance and structure during PD on how to use those materials, to positively influence their instructional practice. medical trainees in procedural specialties

risk recognition
procedural preparedness

title: Quantitative tally-based assessment as a complement to subjective Likert-scale debriefing tools
description: The article proposes a complementary quantitative approach to debriefing assessment, arguing that existing tools like DASH and OSAD are "relatively time consuming and use subjective scales" and are prone to response biases such as socially desirable or extreme responding. The DART replaces subjective scales with cumulative counts of questions, statements and trainee responses, avoiding response bias and reducing complexity, and is intended to provide a conversational substrate for peer feedback and coaching.

constraints: The authors state they do not claim lecturing or lack of questions by debriefers are universal behaviors, and what DART ratio scores represent in terms of true debriefing quality has not been clarified

citation: Riggs C. Daniel, Kang Sohee, Rennie Olivia. (2020). Positive Impact of Multiple-Choice Question Authoring and Regular Quiz Participation on Student Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education 19(2):ar16. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-09-0189
title: Quizzical: an LTI-compliant online MCQ authoring, learning, and self-assessment tool
description: Quizzical is a turnkey, Learning Tools Interoperability-compliant application deployed within a learning management system in a ~500-student sophomore molecular biology course. "Quizzical has two major features: student authoring of MCQs and the use of these questions by students as learning tools and to get relevant practice quizzes for formal examinations." Students author questions categorized as Recall or Application with justifications and textbook images, TAs grade and return flawed questions for editing, and quiz takers see justifications after answering. About 15% of exam questions were student-authored or modified, and student questions earned biserial values of 0.25–0.38.
requirements: Instructor setup schedules authoring and quiz windows, TA grading assignments, and optional participation marks; students log in through the course page and must give permission for their questions to be reused.
constraints: The article notes MCQs are not useful for testing higher-order cognitive processes such as judgment/creativity as defined in Bloom's taxonomy.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: mastery of course topics through self-assessment and retrieval practice
deeper engagement with course content through question authoring
examples: In the reported deployment, students authored two questions each (more than 740 questions per term) and attempted over 400 questions each per term.

knowledge gain
active participation in tutorial groups

title: Expect student question-writing to benefit learning mainly when question quality is high enough
description: The article proposes that the learning benefit of student question generation depends on question quality: "It is likely that the beneficial learning effect of this intervention is evident only if they are good enough." It links question formulation to reflection and metacognition, noting this "effect may require a minimal effort." The authors recommend future studies explore integrating MCQ design into daily work to increase effort, since last-minute writing was probably accompanied by small effort.

Sufficient student effort, possibly fostered by integrating question design into daily work rather than last-minute work

A positive effect was not found in all comparisons, and other authors have not found benefits of MCQ writing

large-class university students
target_learning_goals: deeper understanding of assessed course topics
metacognitive development

citation: Jenny Mirjam Annina, Keller Niklas, Gigerenzer Gerd. (2018). Assessing minimal medical statistical literacy using the Quick Risk Test: a prospective observational study in Germany. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-020847
title: The Quick Risk Test: a 10-item multiple-choice test of minimal medical statistical literacy
description: The Quick Risk Test is a frugal 10-item multiple-choice instrument measuring what the authors define as minimal medical statistical literacy, covering "sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, prevalence, Bayes rule, relative risk, mortality rate, lead time-bias and overdiagnosis bias". It was designed to be applicable to all professional groups in healthcare, unlike earlier discipline-specific instruments, and its primary outcome measure is the number of correct answers out of four multiple-choice alternatives per item. The article reports it can identify knowledge gaps and track performance improvement in risk literacy training, and it was applied to final-year medical students and senior educators. The authors state it is "the first test to measure minimal medical statistical literacy in physicians across disciplines".
requirements: Administered as multiple-choice items reflecting standard medical assessment to enable quick scoring
constraints: Geared towards assessing basic medico-statistical knowledge in medical practitioners; additional tools would be needed for patients
No parallel instruments for convergent validity were tested at the same time
target_learners: final-year medical students
professors, senior physicians and university lecturers of medicine
target_learning_goals: understanding of 10 elementary medical statistical concepts for evaluating medical tests, treatments and screening
examples: Administered before and after a 90-minute training session to 169 final-year students at Charité, and once to 16 senior educators in a CME workshop

title: QUESTOURnament competitive e-learning tool with variable scoring system
description: QUESTOURnament is a Moodle module that lets teachers organize contests of time-constrained intellectual challenges. The article states that "Students obtain points both by answering the proposed challenges and by submitting new questions and assessing the answers submitted by their classmates." Its variable scoring system increases linearly until the first correct answer, then decreases toward zero at the challenge's end, and the system permanently displays an updated five-top ranking. In this study it was used in four individual, non-anonymous contests during a Human Immunology semester.

constraints: In this study QUESTOURnament activities accounted for only 5% of the students' final score

citation: Scott M. Cohen. (2008). Visualizing Teleportation. https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.0051
title: Quantum-coin analogy as a pedagogical device for quantum probabilities
description: The article builds its explanation on 'quantum coins', two-level systems contrasted with classical coins. Readers first see that classical coin states allow certain prediction, then that quantum coins permit states "half H and half T" with probabilistic outcomes, e.g. ⟨H|Q⟩ = 1/2 meaning yes with probability 1/2. The author deliberately overlooks the distinction between probabilities and probability amplitudes "for the beneﬁt of the layperson to whom these ideas are aimed". Only four simple equations are needed for the whole treatment.
requirements: The reader need only accept that certain bracket objects equal 1 or 0; all further discussion follows from the four basic statements about H and T states.
constraints: The probability-amplitude distinction is consciously omitted, so the treatment cannot convey that feature of quantum mechanics.
target_learners: non-mathematically inclined laypeople
target_learning_goals: understanding quantum measurement probabilities
distinguishing classical from quantum states
examples: The two-coin section shows ⟨H1T2|H1H2⟩ = (1)×(0) = 0 to introduce joint questions about multiple coins before entanglement is introduced.

article_title: Real-world ballistics: A dropped bucket
citation: David W. Hogg. (2007). Real-world ballistics: A dropped bucket. https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.0107
title: Any solution of a falling-object problem must quantitatively justify ignoring the air
description: The lecture argues that solving a near-surface fall problem without quantitatively assessing the effect of the air has failed as physics: "The use of the no-air equations is an exercise in mathematics, not physics." The recommended practice is to identify the relevant physical effects, compare air resistance and buoyancy forces to gravity, and only then adopt the no-air equations, checking the justification after an initial calculation. This turns a rote exercise into genuine physical reasoning.
requirements: Learners must be able to estimate air density and compare the ram-pressure force to gravity quantitatively
constraints: The lecture notes pathological situations exist where the assume-air-doesn't-matter-then-check approach will not work
target_learners: Physics students and teachers of introductory mechanics
target_learning_goals: Judging the applicability of idealized equations to real situations
examples: The lecture computes Fa/Fg ≈ ρAh/m for the bucket and finds the empty bucket fails the criterion while the full bucket passes, before using the no-air solution

title: Quantum Tunneling and Wave Packets simulation (PhET)
description: An interactive computer simulation developed as part of the Physics Education Technology Project (PhET). It offers interactive visual models of tunneling of wave packets and plane waves, "allowing students to change the potential and total energies by dragging on the graph" and to view "the real part, imaginary part, magnitude, and phase of the wave function", with energy and wave function displayed on separate graphs to address student confusion between the two.
requirements: The article uses it to begin instruction with wave packets rather than plane waves, so that students can develop a visual model of what is happening in time and space in quantum tunneling.
target_learners: students in transformed modern physics courses for engineering majors
target_learning_goals: developing a visual model of quantum tunneling in time and space
distinguishing wave function representations from energy representations
examples: In the transformed curriculum, instruction began with wave packets rather than plane waves, using the simulation's interactive visual models.
